item.title: Sept. 11 Shaped Their Lives, but They Don’t Remember It.
item.description:
“There was no first time I heard about it. As a child it was simply a fact of the world I was in: 9/11 happened, and people like me are supposed to be sorry for it forever.” — Khalid El-Halabi, 24

“There was no first time I heard about it. As a child it was simply a fact of the world I was in: 9/11 happened, and people like me are supposed to be sorry for it forever.”

— Khalid El-Halabi, 24

“I feel impostor syndrome. It’s not quite apathy; it’s definitely a respect for what happened, but just sort of an understanding that we can’t really be a part of that collective grief.” — Loulou Marmalade Toledano, 17

“I feel impostor syndrome. It’s not quite apathy; it’s definitely a respect for what happened, but just sort of an understanding that we can’t really be a part of that collective grief.”

— Loulou Marmalade Toledano, 17

“My dad’s life has been so affected by it. My mom’s life has been so affected by it. Almost every adult I knew growing up was so affected by what happened, but I don’t have any recollection of it. It doesn’t feel like something that happened to me.” — Julie Frey, 26

Supported by

They have no memory of the buildings missing from the skyline or airports without security lines. But they have strong feelings about how to regard the legacy of the attacks.

By Maia Coleman and Troy Closson

Photographs by Elinor Kry

Maia Coleman and Troy Closson talked to nearly three dozen people 26-years-old and under about what the anniversary means to them. Neither of the reporters have any memory of Sept. 11, though both were alive.

More than 100 million people in the United States today were not alive on the morning the twin towers fell. Millions more were just learning to walk or starting preschool that day.

For them, Sept. 11 exists only in other people’s telling. And if the adults in their lives can vividly recall the way life halted at 8:46 a.m., interviews with nearly three dozen teenagers and adults under 26 revealed a far less singular experience of growing up in the years that followed.

There were 20-year-olds whose worldview was shaped by scenes of death and rubble in Iraq, Iran and Afghanistan. Teenagers who struggled to see Sept. 11 as monumental having grown up amid mass shootings and a pandemic that killed more than 1.2 million Americans.

And college students — from Lower Manhattan to 2,500 miles from ground zero — who described a profound heartache at the scale and breadth of loss that day, even without their own connection it.

“I’m just trying to fundamentally understand something that I feel pretty disconnected from. It’s hard to feel sad about something that you don’t remember.”

Annika Heegaard, 25, who was raised in Williamsburg, Brooklyn and works in strategic communications

Annika Heegaard, 25, has lived her life in the shadow of the attacks. To her, the day feels like something foggy, but looming; always there, but just out of reach.

Trying to connect to Sept. 11, has become something of an obsession for Ms. Heegaard, who now lives on the Upper West Side of Manhattan and considers her identity as a New Yorker a defining characteristic.

Every September, she immerses herself in whatever primary sources she can find: a shaky video of the first plane careening into the steel building. A list of companies headquartered at 1 World Trade. Testimony from emergency workers. Building floor plans. Photographs. Obituaries.

“I can wrap my head around it,” Ms. Heegaard said. “But it doesn’t entirely make sense.”

Today, history teachers in their first year at a middle school might have learned about Sept. 11 as history themselves.

The youngest candidates for Congress never knew airports without security lines.

And if students were taught about Sept. 11 at all, it was often a brief mention in the fall.

So many of them learned outside the classroom: in stories from their siblings and Twitch streamers, podcasts, the Broadway musical “Come From Away,” Instagram memes and photographs of relatives posing before mountains of rubble.

Julie Frey, 26, who splits her time between New York City and New Haven while she pursues a joint degree in law and environmental management

Julie Frey, 26, whose father was a New York police officer on Sept. 11, often wondered what that day had been like for him. But her father, who retired from the force in 2011 and later served in the Navy, refused to talk about it. She remembers him taking a trip every September to avoid the anniversary and the memories that accompany it.

“He doesn’t want to even be reminded of it in any type of capacity,” Ms. Frey said.

She has struggled to understand her parents’ feelings about the attacks.

JD Moussally, a 14-year-old from Flushing, Queens, said hearing about Sept. 11 felt like taking in decades-old sports highlights.

His father talks about classic Knicks, Mets and Rangers games like they happened yesterday — recalling the players, the scores, the emotions of everyone he watched alongside. “I can look up the stats,” Mr. Moussally said. “But that is not the same as remembering the game.”

JD Moussally, 14, a student at St. Francis Preparatory School who lives in the Queens neighborhood of Flushing

For others, the holes in their generation’s memory became more apparent as they grew older.

Elizabeth Cavanagh, 20, a student who was raised on Long Island’s South Shore and whose mother worked at the World Trade Center in 1993 when a van bomb exploded, recalled reciting the Hail Mary with her Catholic school classmates throughout every Sept. 11 anniversary.

But when she went to college at the University of Pittsburgh, only an hour and a half from where Flight 93 had crashed, the anniversary passed unceremoniously.

She wondered: What about the strangers who comforted each other on the streets? What about the firefighters and police officers who risked their lives?

“It’s a story of New York that you see in so many different ways — and that we’re losing over time,” Ms. Cavanagh said.

She and others lamented that the only account they have heard of their country coming together was during one of its worst tragedies — and before they were even born. Today, many said, the country is too divided and our politics too fractured.

“We lost something that day that can’t be measured,” said Joseph Smith, 22, who lives in Northern Virginia and whose older sister joined the Marines after Sept. 11. He believes the attacks made Americans more distrustful and divided.

“We as a country didn’t heal — and we still haven’t healed — from all the things that have happened since 2000.”

Young people across the country have watched their parents and teachers turn stony and quiet year after year on Sept. 11. Still, for them, the day feels more like a chapter of history than a part of their lives, the way they imagine Pearl Harbor or the Vietnam War must have felt for the generations before them.

Life, they said, has been defined by more recent chapters, like Donald Trump’s presidency or the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, along with the tragedies pinging incessantly on their phones, on social media and on the news.

“I honestly feel like a lot of people my age may have just kind of gotten numb to seeing horrible things in the news,” said MK Peters, 23, who lives in Milwaukee.

She described how active shooter drills became a normalized part of school days, and how a global pandemic interrupted her teenage years — and forced her and her friends into extended lockdown.

Jessica Hall, 25, who lives in St. Paul, and whose college years were sundered by the coronavirus pandemic, doesn’t remember Sept. 11. But she knows where she was when 20 first graders and six adults were killed in Sandy Hook, Conn. — and when 14 high school students and three staff members were gunned down in Parkland, Fla.

“That was all a defining thing for me more than 9/11,” she said.

For some young adults, however, Sept. 11 evokes something deeply personal, and painful.

“I wish I could see it the way most Americans do."

Mai Quddus, 23, was born in Bangladesh and works in client relations

Mai Quddus, 23, lives near Princeton, N.J. and said her father stopped using his given name, Mohammed, amid a rise in Islamophobia after the attacks. “I haven’t been able to feel that way because of the way others made us feel,” she said.

Loulou Marmalade Toledano, 17, grew up on the Lower East Side of Manhattan, just over a mile from ground zero. But as the child of immigrant parents — her mother from the Philippines and her father from England — the fear and alienation that permeated immigrant communities after the attacks have shaped her own memories.

“My mom sort of understood that if it had been a different group that had hit the towers that day, then you know, that sort of oppression and alienation that came toward Arab Americans and also Muslim Americans could have easily been any other group,” Ms. Toledano said.

Khalid El-Halabi, 24, who was raised in a Muslim household in the Queens neighborhood of Jackson Heights, was a high school track athlete and often ran to the reflecting pools at the World Trade Center site.

“I would just always be hit by this concept of how many people have lost their lives,” he said. “If that day had not happened, maybe I could have been fully American.”

He was named after his great-grandfather, but his grade school classmates mocked him for sharing a first name with Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, the man accused of plotting the attacks. He was pulled for extra screening at U.S. airports starting at age 2.

And he said he spent his life in the city feeling “almost like a second-class citizen,” seeing the normalization of suspicion and hate against Muslims.

Khalid El-Halabi, 24, who grew up in Queens and works at a biotech company

He remains drawn to ground zero, a symbol of the potential to rebuild.

Berkley Pelletier was ready to sign up for the army.

He was only a child, but listening to the phone calls of flight passengers on a trip to the memorial museum in New York moved him that deeply. And as he grew up in Ohio, he said the legacy of Sept. 11 was filtered through a lens of nationalism: “This horrible thing was done to us.”

Then in middle school, he dug deeper into history himself.

“I realized we were doing really horrible things to other people in the name of justice,” Mr. Pelletier, now 23 and working at an international trade consultancy in Washington, D.C., said.

Like Mr. Pelletier, many young adults said the 25th anniversary reminds them most of the country’s shortcomings.

Life after Sept. 11, to them, has brought a drumbeat of costly and damaging policies in which they, only newly of voting age, have had no voice. While facing a warming planet and rising housing costs, they look back and see trillions spent on war and counterterrorism efforts.

Liberty Wilson, 19, a first-year college student from Westchester County, N.Y.

Liberty Wilson, 19, shared much of her worldview with her mother, who was working in Lower Manhattan when the towers collapsed. But as a teenager, Ms. Wilson learned online about covert C.I.A. operations in the Middle East before Sept. 11 and re-evaluated the country’s entire history of intervention.

Ms. Wilson said her mother believes fighting back against terrorism remains urgent. To Ms. Wilson, the takeaway is more complicated.

“It’s important to always carry the memory,” she said. “But there are also greater lessons to take away from it: We were the cause of so much destruction and instability.”

For Aiden Burrus, 18, who grew up in Connecticut, that tension is top of mind.

Mr. Burrus just started college at George Washington University in Washington, three miles from where Flight 77 hit the Pentagon. As the 25th anniversary approaches, he said he feels called to mourn. For what exactly, though, he isn’t sure.

“I remember the people who’ve passed away. I remember the consequences afterward and everyone else that died because of 9/11,” Mr. Burrus said. “We cannot forget this. I know that I cannot forget this.”

He paused for several seconds.

“But I don’t entirely know what that even means because I wasn’t there. I don’t remember it to begin with.”

item.title: Neighbors Rally After a Manhattan Preschool’s Corn Stalks Are Vandalized
item.description:
For months, the children at the Mis Amiguitos preschool in Manhattan had tended to a bundle of corn stalks growing from a patch of dirt on a busy Upper East Side sidewalk, watching with pride as they grew to over seven feet tall.

Then, one Monday morning last month, the children arrived at the school on York Avenue between East 83rd and 84th Streets to a crime scene: The corn had been uprooted and scattered across the pavement.

The day before, surveillance video showed, a man on a bike had approached the corn stalks in broad daylight, dismounted and ripped them out before pedaling off. The police are investigating, but there have been no arrests and no word on a motive, leaving the school and the neighborhood grappling with a seemingly nonsensical act of vandalism.

“I was beyond angry,” said Mily Caballero, the chief executive of Mis Amiguitos, a full-immersion Spanish Montessori program, “and the kids, of course, just didn’t understand why someone would do that.”

The episode not only undid months of work by the students and their teachers, it also underscored the importance, and vulnerability, of the city’s more than 660,000 sidewalk tree beds as canvases for novelty and creativity. In a city where few schools have access to ample green space, a tiny patch of dirt had offered a group of children a connection to nature and a place to make something grow amid the concrete — until a vandal took it from them.

It was not the first time the patch had been vandalized.

The story began five years ago, when a delivery truck jumped the curb outside the school and uprooted a tree, one of many that offered shade to York Avenue, a bustling street lined with shops and restaurants.

New York City encourages residents to help maintain tree wells on public sidewalks, and the teachers at Mis Amiguitos saw the newly barren plot as a blank canvas.

The students planted flowers, pumpkins and herbs. The school’s neighbors noticed, and were delighted.

“The kids were doing such great things with it,” said Jill Feldmann, who has lived in the neighborhood for 45 years. “They planted flowers, the next year sunflowers.”

But this spring, starting in March, the plants came under attack.

“The flowers we did plant were completely stomped on,” Ms. Caballero said, adding that dog excrement was found on the soil.

The teachers and the students replanted, and this time put up barriers. Again, the plants were flattened. Then they added higher barriers and wire — all told, the school spent about $1,000 on equipment to keep vandals at bay. But on three occasions before the corn was planted, one or more people destroyed the small garden.

Undeterred, in April, the students tried again, this time tucking corn kernels into the soil. By August, the stalks had grown taller than most people.

The school integrated the corn into its curriculum, a hands-on way for students to learn about the crop and how to care for it. They watched as birds, squirrels and bees filtered through the stalks. In the fall, they planned to paint the corn for decoration and teach the students about agriculture.

So when Alexandra Wilcox and her son arrived at the school on Aug. 17 to find the corn uprooted, she, like other parents, struggled to explain to him what had happened.

“He was like, ‘What happened to it?’ And I didn’t have an answer,” she said.

The New York Police Department was notified and is investigating, a spokesperson said.

It seemed to be part of a pattern in the neighborhood. On the night of Aug. 15, a man resembling the person who destroyed the corn stalks was captured in footage from a neighbor’s cellphone yanking sunflowers from a tree well about a block west of the school, according to a resident who tended to the flowers.

Then, on Aug. 20, a doorman witnessed someone using what appeared to be a machete to hack at a patch of begonias not far away, on Park Avenue at 66th Street, said Amy Sheldon, the executive director of the Fund for Park Avenue.

As word of the vandalism spread, Ms. Caballero said, an unexpected influx of generosity emerged. Neighbors and business owners reached out with offers of emotional and material support, including a gift card to Home Depot for supplies to fortify the tree bed. An anonymous neighbor also dropped off a bag of flower seeds.

On Aug. 19, the Balloon Saloon in TriBeCa delivered a handful of smiling corn helium balloons, which Mis Amiguitos placed in the tree well where the real corn stalks had stood. But by the next morning, someone had snipped the strings, either absconding with the balloons or letting them float away.

“Here we were trying to do something kind and make the kids hopeful,” said Sharon Hershkowitz, the owner of the Balloon Saloon. “To be bashed again, what message does that tell them?”

In the early evening on Aug. 20, a flash flood warning was issued as a soaking rain deluged York Avenue. Inside Mis Amiguitos, parents bundled their children in rain gear and opened umbrellas. When asked about the corn, Adrian Wilcox, 3, said he was “sad that it’s in the garbage,” but there were signs of hope. Agreeing with an adult, he said, “It’ll work out.”

Parents and teachers shared his optimism.

“It’s a learning lesson,” said Scott Klipper, whose two children attend the school. “Whether it’s part of being in New York City, or a city, this is something to learn and grow from.”

The Balloon Saloon sent a new batch of vegetable inflatables on Aug. 21. Ms. Caballero said that the students would plant marigolds, the sacred flower of Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, the Mexican tradition in which people celebrate and mourn the departed. Instead of tying the balloons outside, each student was sent home with one.

The school placed a sign in the tree bed that week thanking the neighborhood for “overwhelming love, kind words and support” that turned a painful experience into “a powerful lesson in community for the children.”

On a table inside the school, a wicker basket held pieces of the corn stalks that had been collected from the sidewalk. Also tucked inside was a magnifying glass that the children could use to closely inspect the kernels and the veins running through the husks — recasting a traumatic episode as a teaching opportunity.

“We took some of the kernels out, we’re going to plant next week,” Ms. Caballero said. “We’re not giving up.”

item.title: Somewhere, Roy Cohn Is Smiling
item.description:
At this point in the Trumpian arc, we’re all too familiar with the president’s methods: Deny everything; apologize for nothing. Hog the spotlight. Counterattack, counterpunch, countersue. Always declare victory, even when you lose (especially when you lose). Resentment sells. Nativism sells. Cruelty, if not yet normal, becomes the norm. Rules and traditions are for suckers; everyone is, if not corrupt, at least corruptible.

These are President Trump’s instincts, yes. But before they were his, they were Roy Cohn’s.

Kai Bird’s new book, “American Scoundrel,” written with Susan Goldmark (Bird’s wife and chief researcher), is a biography of Cohn, the sinister 20th-century lawyer who served as chief counsel to Joe McCarthy when the junior senator from Wisconsin was Red Scaring America and as lawyer to Trump when the young real estate developer was deflecting allegations of discrimination against prospective Black tenants. “American Scoundrel” is very much a how-we-got-here book, showing how Cohn’s guile, paranoia and shamelessness guided McCarthy, rubbed off on Trump and stuck fast to America.

The day after winning the 2016 election, Trump was on the phone with Roger Stone, his friend and adviser and longtime Cohn ally. “Wouldn’t Roy love to see this moment?” the president-elect said wistfully of Cohn, who died in 1986. “Boy, do we miss him.” And just months later, when the president fumed that Jeff Sessions, then the attorney general, was failing to protect him, an irate Trump demanded, “Where’s my Roy Cohn?”

If he really wanted to find Cohn, all Trump had to do was look in the mirror.

The Cohn-Trump parallels are evident on nearly every page of “American Scoundrel,” so much so that Bird barely needs to point them out. From a young age, for example, Cohn traded on the influence of his father, a New York judge, much as Trump would lean on the wealth and connections of his own father, Fred Trump. At 16, Cohn got one of his high school teachers out of a traffic ticket by calling the police precinct — “I’m sure you know who my father is” — and later relied on paternal clout to secure a job as an assistant U.S. attorney in New York.

Cohn became obsessed with publicizing his accomplishments — “I didn’t count it as winning if the world didn’t know about it” — and cultivated gossip columnists to stay in the headlines. (Not that he needed much help: Cohn’s role in the prosecution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg established his name in legal and anti-Communist circles, even before his work for McCarthy made him a national figure.) To Cohn, “personal loyalty was everything,” Bird writes, and his disregard for legalities was captured in his maxim “Don’t tell me the law. Tell me the judge.”

He was even terrible at paying his bills, “another lesson Trump learned from Cohn,” Bird writes. Like his protégé, Cohn was indicted several times and was constantly under I.R.S. audit. At his birthday party in 1980, friends presented Cohn with a cake featuring his own scowling visage. (No word if T-shirts were available.) People who knew both men recognized that some of Trump’s verbal tics — “if you want to know the truth” and “I can tell you” — trace back to Cohn.

Cohn also liked to talk about crowd size. In 1963, after pleading not guilty to charges of perjury and obstruction of justice, Cohn stood outside a Manhattan courthouse and told the assembled reporters that it was the “biggest crowd I’ve seen since the Army-McCarthy hearings.” And when he gave a party in Washington celebrating Ronald Reagan’s 1980 election, Cohn boasted about the celebrities in attendance (Barbara Walters and Andy Warhol, among others) and bragged that “we had the biggest crowd.”

Oh, and Cohn sported a permanent tan, too.

Beyond style and temperament, Cohn and Trump shared a political template. Cohn “excelled at performative politics,” Bird writes, purporting to stand for the working class while riding around in a Rolls-Royce or hosting parties aboard his yacht, the Defiance. Both men saw history “through a lens tinted by conspiracy,” branding their rivals as Communists, radicals or denizens of the “deep state.” In a 1978 profile by Ken Auletta, which Bird cites, Cohn assails liberals for believing that “we must be loved by the rest of the world, which happens to hate us,” rather than focusing on national interests. “There’s nothing particularly original about Trump’s macho instincts in foreign policy,” Bird argues. They came from Cohn.

“The McCarthyism of the 1950s,” Bird writes, “morphed into a nativist, America Firster politics that transformed the modern Republican Party into a party of resentments against the old establishment, against multiculturalism, globalization and liberal culture” — with Cohn serving as connective tissue between McCarthy and Trump. Reading “American Scoundrel,” I sometimes wondered why the title wasn’t plural.

A journalist who interviewed Cohn at length offered an assessment that could fit Trump just as well: “He harbored a bundle of thinly concealed prejudices that he’d trot out whenever one or more of them worked for him, whenever they were useful.” The question for our time is: How long might they prove useful?

“Roy Cohn’s McCarthyism would long outlast McCarthy and would poison the American political landscape for decades to come,” Bird writes. Trumpism, too, may mutate and endure, even when Trump himself — weighed down by war, worn down by low public approval, slowed down by age — begins to recede from view.

“Why was McCarthy discredited but not McCarthyism?” Bird asks. In part, he concludes, it was because President Dwight Eisenhower declined to attack the senator directly, no matter the entreaties of Eisenhower’s advisers, including his younger brother Milton Eisenhower, who urged the president to “tear McCarthy to pieces.” Even as McCarthyism split the country and infected the Republican Party, the president “never took the political risk to ridicule McCarthy’s assumptions,” Bird writes. Eisenhower decided that ignoring the senator was better than elevating him through direct confrontation.

How often have we seen such calculations from Republican leaders during the Trump years, with painful and predictable results? The slide from amusement to dismay to toleration and finally to capitulation has been short but steep, and we may be stuck at the bottom for a while. The paranoia of McCarthyism “persisted as a routine feature of American life,” long after McCarthy exited the stage, Bird writes, leaving “a festering wound on the nation’s psyche.” Trump, under the tutelage of McCarthy’s former aide, learned to pick at that wound, making sure it kept bleeding.

Bird is a chronicler of the American establishment; his prior subjects include presidents like Jimmy Carter, advisers like McGeorge Bundy and scientists like Robert Oppenheimer. Cohn lurked around the edges of these stories, the anti-establishment force who both fed off and sabotaged the establishment. Now, with Trump, Cohn’s politics have won; the establishment has been dispatched, co-opted, emasculated. What remains, Bird writes, is a “subversive counternarrative” of American power.

In an interview with Times reporters early this year, Trump said that the only constraint he felt on his power was, well, himself. “My own morality,” he said. “My own mind. It’s the only thing that can stop me.” Bird does not make this comparison, but Trump’s words evoke Cohn’s, yet again, from a Penthouse interview 45 years ago. “I decided long ago to make my own rules,” he said, “to act according to my own choices, my own judgments and my own conscience.”

Where’s our Roy Cohn? Sitting in the Oval Office.

item.title: How to Stop Cheating in the A.I. Era
item.description:
To the Editor:

Adam Grant’s Aug. 30 guest essay, “To Stop Cheating in School, Address the Root Cause,” argues that the only way to stop cheating in the A.I. era is to instill moral values that make students not want to cheat. But another way to address A.I.-based cheating is to recognize that A.I. is a tool and allow students to use it to complete exams and assignments.

Before A.I., some take-home exams were open book, allowing students to draw on reference material as they saw fit. Students who understood the material and knew how to use reference sources effectively would generally outperform less capable students. Similarly, students who understand the material are more likely to ask A.I. the right questions and to recognize and correct errors in its output.

In my secondary education in the 1970s, electronic calculators were viewed much as A.I. is today. There were fears that students could simply punch buttons and get correct answers without understanding what they were doing. In hindsight, those fears were overblown.

Consider Dr. Grant’s example of a surgeon who cheated through medical school using A.I. I would welcome a surgeon who knows how to use A.I. to learn the latest techniques and who used it as a tool in medical school. I would not, however, attempt to be my own surgeon, regardless of how much A.I. I was allowed to use.

Robert R. MooreDallas

To the Editor:

Adam Grant proposes focusing on “moral identity” as a means of addressing the A.I.-fueled cheating epidemic in schools. I applaud this argument. As a lifelong teacher and scholar, though, I fear that the solution has a snowflake’s chance of working.

Moral behavior depends greatly on the behavior of others in the same environment. I witnessed isolated incidents of cheating among my peers in high school and college, and I never felt tempted to copy their choices because they were so isolated. I thought of myself as a good person.

What would I have done if I knew that 10 percent of my classmates were cheating? Or 50 percent? Or more? Would the rewards of a positive self-image have persuaded me to abandon the arms race? I hope so, but many righteous young people have evidently now arrived at a different conclusion.

Moral identity is not binary; it exists along a spectrum. It is also situational. People who are “mostly moral” sometimes make seemingly immoral decisions when threatened, disadvantaged or otherwise harmed by their peers. Game theory suggests that A.I. disarmament based on the principle of academic morality will be exceedingly difficult to achieve.

Andrew WilliamsonHong Kong

To the Editor:

Having spent my life teaching at highly selective colleges and universities, I sympathize with Adam Grant’s plea that we do something about the temptation to cheat — greatly exacerbated in recent days by A.I. And I agree with him that establishing moral identities in people will help.

But I quarrel with his suggestion that the lack of moral identity is the root cause of the problem. When elite schools boast about, and get credit for, rejecting 95 percent of applicants, the pressure to cheat becomes overwhelming. When companies boast about getting 500 applicants for every job, the pressure to cheat is overwhelming. When young employees see cheating by their colleagues rewarded with promotions and bonuses, the pressure to cheat is overwhelming.

What is rewarded is return on investment, not honor and integrity.

So let us, by all means, work to nurture moral identities, but let us also work to relieve the pressure on young people. I have proposed using a lottery among the qualified for college admissions and jobs. Under such a system, one needs to be good enough … and lucky.

This is how the system already runs, but people pretend otherwise. It will be a lot easier to encourage people to do the right thing when the price they pay for strong moral identities is made a great deal lower.

Barry SchwartzOakland, Calif.The writer is a co-author of “Practical Wisdom: The Right Way to Do the Right Thing.”

To the Editor:

Re “The App That’s Bringing Disabled Daters Together” (Science Times, Aug. 25):

How refreshing to read about an app that opens the world of romance to disabled people (and unprejudiced able-bodied ones as well).

The digital world in general is a huge boon for disabled people, since if you can move a muscle, you can get online. This illustrates how the anti-digital mind-set is extremely ableist — in effect if not in intent.

Felicia Nimue AckermanProvidence, R.I.
